summary: Round 3 of M4.8c, scoped to the delta since b7e295cc9053. Both round-2 majors are closed and I measured each kill individually in a copy of the staged bytes rather than reading the prose. R2b: hoisting `written = true` above the pointer PUT now fails exactly one test, aFailedPOINTERWriteLeavesTheCheckpointUNWRITTENSoALaterTriggerRedoesBoth (288 sequencer tests, 1 failed) -- the tick-driven shape is the right one, since a second commit re-arms `dirty` on its own. The writer's pointer epoch is also killed: `new LogKeys(keys.prefix(), 1).latestCheckpointKey()` fails theWriterPutsThePointerUnderITSOwnEpochsPrefix with the epoch-1 key in the message. Invariants.readChain's filter is pinned in the deletion direction too: removing `if (!keys.isEntryKey(...)) continue;` fails theInvariantCheckerToleratesCheckpointsBesideTheChain. Full suite green at 776 tests, matching the row's claim exactly. R2a: I checked every clause of the rewritten newestCheckpoint paragraph against the sources rather than accepting it -- `start` does take `won.get().epoch()` (LocalSequencer.java:255) and epochs advance by exactly one per acquisition, M4.6e's row does record restart/rolling-deploy/TTL-expiry/failed-start each burning one, M4.9's notes row does say 'AND IT MUST BOUND THE CROSSING, not merely own-chain replay', and M4.6e's cost paragraph does state the transitive crossing as O(all commit-log entries ever written). The actionable steer is now correct. R2c: the invented M4.9-sequence dependency is gone from the ADR and, checked by grep, from every other site in the tree -- no leftover assertion of it, which is the M4.8b2 failure mode avoided. failNextPointerPut does not disturb the existing injectors: separate one-shot field, `/LATEST` predicate disjoint from `.ckpt`, no existing test arms it, and it throws before delegating so the object genuinely does not land. Cost shape unchanged by this delta: no production request added or moved, discovery is still stat+get whatever the history, a checkpoint is still two PUTs per trigger scaling with neither streams nor pods. Four minors, none blocking: a false claim about list-and-take-last still standing in a test comment that this commit's own LogKeys correction retracts; a measured surviving mutation behind a newly widened `.as()` label; the rounds: entry claiming the cost argument survived untouched when two of its stated reasons did not; and two imprecise clauses inside the corrected paragraph's self-correction. A note not filed as a finding: the ADR's surviving ground 'they are the ordered history M7's retention prunes' is circular as a reason to write them -- we would write them so M7 can delete them -- but it is paired with 'and an operator reads', and the paragraph now concedes 'an audit trail and nothing else', so it is honestly argued.

findings.title: This commit retracts list-and-take-last in LogKeys and leaves the identical claim standing in a test comment two files away
findings.detail: The staged LogKeys.checkpointKeyFor javadoc now says, in as many words, '⚠️ M4.9 DOES NOT FIND THE NEWEST BY TAKING THE LAST OF THESE, and an earlier version of this sentence said it did -- that is the `list`-and-take-last mechanism ADR-0034 rejects. It reads latestCheckpointKey.' CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:245-247, untouched by this commit, still states the retracted claim as the REASON the padding test exists: 'COUNT CANNOT SEE THIS: `Long.toHexString(seq)` leaves every count identical while `10.ckpt` sorts before `9.ckpt` -- and M4.9 bounds replay by taking the LAST key under the prefix.' That is now false in the tree, and it is the third site of a claim this task has corrected twice already (once in LogKeys, once in ADR-0034's alternative as R2c). It is exactly the shape M4.8b2's own baselines entry records and calls out as needing correction AT THE SITE: 'review found the retracted putIfAbsent rationale still asserted at its own site in backlog-done.md' and 'the NFR-2 argument left standing in a TEST javadoc after production retracted it'. The replacement reason already exists in the corrected LogKeys javadoc -- 'the padding still matters, because the seq-keyed objects are the ordered history M7 prunes'.
findings.suggestion: Replace the '-- and M4.9 bounds replay by taking the LAST key under the prefix' clause with the ground LogKeys now gives: the seq-keyed objects are the ordered history M7's retention prunes and an operator reads, so their key order must be numeric order.
findings.failure_scenario: Whoever builds M4.9 opens the checkpoint tests to see what is already pinned, reads that M4.9 'bounds replay by taking the LAST key under the prefix', and implements discovery as list-and-take-last -- the mechanism ADR-0034 exists to reject and the one M4.0's rounds 2 and 3 each caught. The strict zero-LIST assertion in CheckpointDiscoveryTest would catch it if they wrote a new test in that file, but nothing forces them to; what they would have is a green suite and a comment in the tree telling them the naive form is what M4.9 does.

findings.title: The `.as()` label widened this round claims 'not per request', and the fixture cannot make that discrimination -- measured surviving
findings.detail: The only production-facing change in this file's existing test is the label: 'one pointer PUT per trigger -- not per stream, not per pod' became '... not per stream, not per pod, not per request'. The assertion behind it is unchanged, `assertThat(store.pointerKeys()).hasSize(2)` after two triggers. 'not per stream' is genuinely pinned -- the second commitOne passes streams=3. 'not per pod' is genuinely pinned -- by the second trigger `pods` holds poda and podb, so a per-pod PUT would give 1+2=3. 'not per request' is not pinned at all: commitOne builds `List.of(new CommitRequest(...))`, a single element, for both calls, so a pointer PUT issued once per CommitRequest emits exactly 1 per trigger and 2 in total. MEASURED in a copy of the staged bytes: capturing `requests.size()` on the commit thread beside pendingStreams and wrapping `store.put(keys.latestCheckpointKey(), ...)` in `for (int i = 0; i < pendingRequests; i++)` leaves the WHOLE suite green -- `./gradlew test --rerun-tasks`, BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 776 tests, zero <failure> elements. This is the 'a replacement criterion that asserts a code path it does not reach' mode M4.8b's own baselines entry records as its third failure mode.
findings.suggestion: Either give one of the two commitOne calls a second CommitRequest -- two pod flushes batched into one delta is what M4.7 built and what a per-request PUT would multiply -- so hasSize(2) actually separates per-trigger from per-request, or drop 'not per request' from the label and leave the claim at what the fixture measures.
findings.failure_scenario: A later change moves the pointer write somewhere it can see the request list -- the obvious one is folding the pointer maintenance into `capture`, which already iterates `requests` for `pods.merge` -- and issues one PUT per request. The suite stays green and the assertion message states in the report that per-request was checked. In production one commitAll batches every contributing pod flush in the window (M4.7's row: 'the PER-POD one that has to be built and asserted'), so the checkpoint pointer's PUT rate becomes one per pod flush per trigger instead of one per trigger, multiplying the rate the ADR prices at two PUTs per trigger by the window fan-in, and doing it silently because the only assertion that would have caught it says it already did.

findings.title: The rounds: entry claims the cost argument survived every round untouched; two of the cost arguments are what the rounds actually corrected
findings.detail: The opening clause reads 'THE MECHANISM AND ITS COST ARGUMENT SURVIVED EVERY ROUND UNTOUCHED -- the pointer, the body-not-sequence choice, `stat`-before-`get`, the lease rejection, two PUTs per trigger'. Every one of those five DECISIONS did survive; I re-checked each against the sources. But two of the ARGUMENTS for them did not. Round 2's R2a was filed against a cost argument in production javadoc -- 'a chain-wide answer across an ancestry would cost one stat per ancestor epoch, and nothing needs it' -- and the finding's own text says 'the cost clause also compares in the wrong direction'; that paragraph is rewritten in this very delta. Round 2's R2c was filed against the stated cost/benefit ground for 'two PUTs per trigger' -- the ADR's rejection of the one-PUT alternative rested on an M4.9 dependency that does not exist -- and that ground is rewritten in this very delta to 'an audit trail and nothing else'. The entry does record both corrections lower down, so the reader is not deceived about events; the headline is what is wrong. The distinction the M4.8b2 entry three lines above in this same file draws correctly is the phrasing available: 'Every decision survived review; no reason did.'
findings.suggestion: Narrow the clause to what held: the five DECISIONS survived every round untouched, and two of their stated reasons did not -- the per-ancestor cost clause at newestCheckpoint and the ADR's ground for the second PUT -- which is the same pattern M4.8b2's entry names four times.
findings.failure_scenario: baselines/review.txt is the only trace in the tree of why this task went past the two-round cap, and it is read by whoever next argues an exception. A headline saying the cost argument survived untouched, against a task whose round 2 filed a major and a minor against exactly two cost arguments, teaches that the rounds were spent on test strength alone -- so the next author checks their tests against the sources and not their cost prose, which is where this task's round 2 found both defects. It also understates the case for the third round it is arguing for.

findings.title: The corrected newestCheckpoint paragraph contradicts itself about which half of the old claim was false, and calls an O(ancestors) walk cheap without saying it is not constant
findings.detail: Two clauses, both inside the self-correction rather than the steer. (1) 'AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS PARAGRAPH SAID THE OPPOSITE -- that a chain-wide answer costs one stat per ancestor and "nothing needs it". Both halves were false.' The second half was false. The first was arithmetically correct and the paragraph says so two sentences later: 'The per-ancestor stat is the CHEAP side'. Round 2's finding did not say the cost figure was false either -- it said 'the cost clause also compares in the wrong direction'. What was wrong was the conclusion drawn from a correct number, which is a different and more useful lesson than the number being wrong. (2) 'The per-ancestor stat is the CHEAP side' is true relative to what it replaces and incomplete as guidance: cheap is not bounded. One stat per ancestor is O(epochs walked), and M4.6e's row records that every restart, rolling deploy, TTL expiry and failed start burns an epoch, that nothing compacts them, and that 20,000 terms must recover fine -- a store outage spanning failovers burns many at once. M4.9's row asks for a BOUND, and 'constant in checkpoint count' is the discriminator this very task chose over 'zero LISTs' for exactly the reason that a cheaper-than-before rate is not a bounded one.
findings.suggestion: Say the earlier version's cost figure was right and its conclusion was not, which is the checkable form; and note that a per-ancestor stat is cheap but not constant, so M4.9's bound has to be stated on something other than 'fewer requests than today' -- the same trap the row records M4.0's rounds falling into twice with the page-count bound.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.9 is built against this javadoc, walks the ancestry issuing one stat per ancestor, measures it against today's transitive GET-per-entry crossing, finds it dramatically cheaper and lands it as 'bounded recovery'. After a store outage that burns a run of epochs -- the case M4.6e's row exists to document, and the case ChainReplay.firstInheritableAncestor's own javadoc says it walks -- takeover cost is again linear in the cluster's failover history rather than constant, and the assertion guarding it passes because it was written as a comparison against the old code rather than as a constant across two ancestry depths. That is the page-count weakening in a new dimension, and the ADR the same commit adds is the record that would be relied on.
